Abstract
Highlights
What are the main findings?
Effective CAV controllability depends on spatial availability, HDV response, platoon organization, and information and computation quality—not on penetration alone.
Cross-scale resilience requires coupling vehicle/platoon actuation with signal, routing, and regional traffic control while evaluating service retention, cumulative loss, and recovery time.
What are the implications of the main findings?
V2X quality should be treated as a control constraint that triggers graded cooperation, safe fallback, and re-synchronization rather than as an ideal communication assumption.
Deployment evidence should progress from simulation to real-data, SIL/HIL, and field validation under reproducible physical and communication disturbances.
Abstract
Connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) are emerging as mobile sensing and actuation resources in mixed traffic, but their contribution to urban road-network resilience depends on more than nominal penetration. This structured critical review examines how local CAV sensing and control can be translated into effective controllability and measurable recovery across vehicle, intersection, corridor, and network scales. An auditable pre-submission update retrieved 1601 raw records from the Web of Science Core Collection, ScienceDirect, and IEEE Xplore and yielded 1476 unique auditable candidates after deduplication. This update identified 66 incremental relevant records, which were combined with the earlier 202-study evidence pool to form a 268-record corpus for the final synthesis. The

9.7. Limitations of the Review
This review has seven principal limitations. First, it is a structured critical review rather than a registered systematic review; the 2026 WoS/ScienceDirect/IEEE update is auditable, but early database-by-database Scopus/TRID logs cannot be reconstructed fully, so exhaustive coverage is not claimed. The original review workflow did not employ dual independent screening or a prospectively defined inter-reviewer agreement protocol; consequently, formal Cohen’s
κ
statistics are not reported. Borderline records were resolved through author discussion, but some judgment remains unavoidable in a structured critical review. Similarly, the E0–E4 ladder is used as a qualitative interpretation framework rather than an exhaustive numerical classification of all records, and the CiteSpace modularity/silhouette values are descriptive network diagnostics without null-model significance testing. Second, simulation platforms, demand, penetration, disturbance design, baselines, and metrics vary substantially, making reported percentage improvements non-comparable. Third, much of the evidence remains E0–E2 despite increasing real-data, testbed, HIL, and engineering-platform work; evidence on E3–E4 urban-network resilience remains scarce. Fourth, the E0–E4 scale and the control-quality contract are author-defined synthesis tools and have not been externally standardized. Fifth, the 268-record candidate list contains sufficient bibliographic information for year, venue, and author-frequency summaries but not complete affiliation or citation metadata; conse

10. Conclusions
The reviewed evidence indicates that CAV penetration should be interpreted as potential rather than automatically realized control authority. The strongest evidence currently concerns mixed-platoon stabilization, vehicle-level disturbance attenuation, and intersection/corridor efficiency. Network-level resilience additionally depends on where controllable vehicles are located, what traffic and infrastructure states remain observable, how HDVs respond, whether communication and computation support the intended cooperation mode, and whether local actions are coordinated with signal, routing, perimeter, and residual-capacity control.
The literature is considerably less mature for closed-loop network recovery under simultaneous physical and information-layer disturbances. Self-sensing UHPC illustrates a possible additional infrastructure-state sensing layer, but the reviewed material studies do not yet demonstrate a complete material-signal–traffic-control–network-recovery loop. It is therefore treated as a prospective observability interface rather than established evidence of resilience improvement.
Accordingly, the effective-controllability indicators, communication-aware control-quality contract, and E0–E4 evidence ladder proposed in this review should be interpreted as author-defined synthesis tools rather than externally validated standards.
